summary: Ottawa City Council held a marathon session on September 15th 2023 and approved a broad infrastructure plan covering roads, bridges, public buildings, LRT expansion and green infrastructure. The plan aims to reshape the city over coming decades while meeting environmental and economic sustainability principles. Councillors outlined specific projects, timelines and rationales for each area.
one_line: Ottawa City Council approved a wide infrastructure plan on September 15th 2023 covering roads, bridges, a library, community center, LRT Phase 3 and green projects.
key_facts: Ottawa City Council held a marathon session running well into the evening on September 15th 2023 to devise an infrastructure enhancement plan.

Councillor Jessica LeBlanc said the road plan targets roads that haven't seen major updates since the late 90s, under a five-year plan meant to reduce vehicle wear and tear, improve commute times and lower traffic-related incidents.
Merivale Road will be expanded to alleviate its long-standing bottleneck.
The Hunt Club corridor will be modernized to handle anticipated traffic increases from future suburban development projects.
Engineering assessments of Ottawa's aging bridges will begin in October 2023.
Prince of Wales Bridge is set for a comprehensive renovation starting in the spring of 2024.
The Ottawa Central Library, a joint initiative between Library and Archives Canada and City of Ottawa, is scheduled to break ground in 2024 with environmentally sustainable features.
Barrhaven residents unveiled plans for a multi-purpose community center combining indoor sports facilities, event spaces, council services and construction-phase employment.
Phase 3 of the LRT expansion will bring rail service to southern and western suburbs, with increased oversight and contractor accountability, according to Councillor David Chen.
The LRT expansion was one of the more controversial agenda items, resolved after lengthy discussion and heated exchanges following problems with the initial roll-out.
The Council allocated substantial funds to green infrastructure, including more efficient street lighting, green spaces along redesigned roadways and bike lanes.
Councillor Rhonda James said "The age of single-occupancy, gas-powered commuting is coming to an end" and noted younger Ottawans' interest in environmental stewardship.
